entry.title: Beyond sectors: what groups do US stocks really form?

link.title: Beyond sectors: what groups do US stocks really form?

entry.content:
Stocks are usually grouped by industry. But which stocks actually move together, once the market as a whole is taken out? I fitted a Bayesian stochastic block model, a statistical model of group structure that I also use for ecological food webs, to the co-movement network of 250 large US stocks from 2010 to 2026.

The model finds a few dozen groups that refine sectors to roughly the sub-industry level. The interesting part is how they change:

  • in the 2020 COVID crash, stocks regrouped across sectors by their exposure to lockdowns and reopening, and the share of a stock’s group-mates from other sectors jumped from 39% to 63%;
  • the 2022 rise in interest rates left sectors intact;
  • used to build low-risk portfolios, the groups give a small improvement over standard methods.

More on the project page; code on GitHub.
entry.summary: A Bayesian stochastic block model finds groups of stocks that refine industry sectors, and shows how COVID briefly broke them apart.

entry.title: How heavy are the tails of financial returns?

link.title: How heavy are the tails of financial returns?

entry.content:
How likely is a daily loss bigger than any seen so far? The answer depends on the shape of the tail of the return distribution, and the usual tests of that shape are unreliable for the small samples that tails provide.

Constrained surrogates, a recent method from Moore and Altmann, test a whole family of tail shapes without estimating any parameter. The idea is like shuffling: rearrange the tail values while keeping fixed the one summary the fit depends on, and compare the data with the results. I implemented the method, checked it on simulated data, and applied it to 22 assets across six asset classes. In short:

  • thin, exponential-like tails are rejected for most assets’ losses, but rarely for their gains;
  • a single power law describes only the most extreme few percent of days;
  • losses tend to be heavier-tailed than gains;
  • the method sharpens how tail models are checked, but it does not improve one-day value-at-risk forecasts.

More on the project page; code on GitHub.
entry.summary: Testing power-law, lognormal and exponential tails for 22 assets, without estimating a single parameter.

entry.title: An overnight price floor in the Counter-Strike 2 skin market

link.title: An overnight price floor in the Counter-Strike 2 skin market

entry.content:
On 22 October 2025, Valve changed Counter-Strike 2’s trade-up rules so that five Covert skins can be exchanged for one knife or pair of gloves. That made every eligible Covert worth at least a fifth of the expected value of the knife or glove it could become: if it traded for less, buying five and trading up would pay on average.

It is a rare clean natural experiment in no-arbitrage pricing. Using public prices, I found that:

  • today, no eligible skin trades clearly below its floor;
  • skins that were below their new floor before the update were lifted onto it by almost exactly the size of the gap;
  • the adjustment happened within about a day, and the floor then spread one tier down through the older trade-up rules.

The full write-up is on the project page, and the code is on GitHub.
entry.summary: A game update turned some skins into lottery tickets on knives, and prices found the implied floor within a day.
